skills.presentation: Persistent cough and sputum production for more than 2 weeks, or accompanied by blood-streaked sputum/hemoptysis, afternoon low-grade fever (37.4-38.0℃), night sweats, fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.

first_questions: How long have you had the cough and sputum? Has it lasted more than 2 weeks?
Have you noticed blood streaks in your sputum, or have you coughed up fresh blood?
Do you have a fever (low-grade) every afternoon or evening? Do you wake up at night with your clothes and bedding soaked with sweat (night sweats)?
followup_questions: Have you had significant weight loss recently?
Have you had contact at home or work with someone with pulmonary tuberculosis or a similar long-term cough?
Have you ever had diabetes, HIV infection, or long-term use of glucocorticoids or immunosuppressants?
stop_conditions: Cough duration, hemoptysis volume, and afternoon low-grade fever, night sweats, and constitutional wasting symptoms have been clarified
History of tuberculosis contact and risk factors for immunocompromise have been obtained
Prior anti-tuberculosis history and adherence to standardized treatment have been clearly assessed

essential: High-resolution chest CT/DR chest radiograph (to assess exudative, proliferative, caseous necrotic, cavitary, and disseminated lesions in the apical posterior segment of the upper lobe or the superior segment of the lower lobe)
Sputum acid-fast bacillus smear microscopy (submit 3 consecutive specimens)
Molecular testing of sputum for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (GeneXpert MTB/RIF, rapid detection of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance)
Tuberculosis-specific cell-mediated immune response test (T-SPOT.TB or interferon-gamma release assay, IGRA)
Liver and kidney function tests and complete blood count (baseline assessment before anti-tuberculosis medication)
if_suspected: Liquid culture of sputum for M. tuberculosis using MGIT, plus species identification and drug susceptibility testing (DST)
Electronic bronchoscopy (GeneXpert testing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid [BALF] for patients unable to produce sputum or with diagnostic difficulty)
avoid: Whole-body bone isotope ECT scanning when multiple bone metastases are not clearly suspected
Empirical use of quinolone antibiotics before the diagnosis is clear (it can mask tuberculosis toxicity and induce resistance)

first_line: For newly diagnosed active pulmonary tuberculosis, follow the ten-character principle: 'early, combined, appropriate dosage, regular, and full-course'

Standard short-course chemotherapy regimen 2HRZE/4HR (intensive phase for the first 2 months with isoniazid [H] + rifampicin [R] + pyrazinamide [Z] + ethambutol [E], followed by continuation phase for 4 months with isoniazid [H] + rifampicin [R]; total course 6 months)
Directly observed treatment, short-course (DOTS) throughout.
safety_warnings: Anti-tuberculosis drugs have significant hepatotoxicity (H, R, and Z can all cause liver injury); liver function must be monitored every 2-4 weeks during treatment; if ALT >3 times the upper limit of normal with jaundice, timely adjustment or discontinuation is required
Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuritis (oral vitamin B6 is needed for prevention); rifampicin can cause orange-red urine and strong enzyme-inducing drug interactions
Ethambutol can cause retrobulbar optic neuritis; closely monitor visual acuity and visual fields during treatment
personalization: Multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (MDR-TB): develop a long-term second-line regimen based on drug susceptibility results, including at least bedaquiline, linezolid, and other agents
Patients with comorbid diabetes: strictly control blood glucose with insulin; the course may be appropriately extended to 9-12 months
Massive hemoptysis emergency: absolute bed rest in the lateral decubitus position on the affected side, maintain airway patency, use pituitrin to stop bleeding, and prevent suffocation

skills.presentation: Chronic infected individuals often have no obvious clinical symptoms; during the active phase, they may present with fatigue, easy fatigability, decreased appetite, aversion to greasy food, nausea, dull pain or discomfort in the right upper quadrant hepatic region, and abdominal distension; during acute or severe exacerbations, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and sclera, dark yellow urine), palmar erythema, spider angiomas, and hepatosplenomegaly may occur.

first_questions: How many years have you been diagnosed with hepatitis B (positive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc, or positive for HBsAg, anti-HBe, and anti-HBc)? Do you usually have regular follow-up at the hospital?
Recently, have you had marked generalized fatigue, no appetite, aversion to greasy food, nausea, or dull right upper abdominal pain?
Have your eyes (whites of the eyes) and skin turned yellow? Is your urine as dark as strong tea?
followup_questions: Are you currently taking antiviral medication regularly by mouth (such as entecavir or tenofovir)? Have you missed doses or stopped the medication on your own?
Do any family members (mother, siblings) have a history of hepatitis B, cirrhosis, or liver cancer?
Do you have a history of heavy alcohol use or concomitant use of liver-damaging drugs?
stop_conditions: The stage of hepatitis B virus infection has been clarified (chronic carrier/active hepatitis/compensated or decompensated cirrhosis)
Prodromal signs of acute liver failure have been ruled out (extreme fatigue, worsening gastrointestinal symptoms, coagulopathy with PTA<40%)
History of antiviral drug use and drug resistance status have been clearly determined

essential: Hepatitis B virus serologic markers (quantitative five-item hepatitis B panel: HBsAg, HBsAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, HBcAb)
High-sensitivity quantitative HBV-DNA (lower limit of detection 10-20 IU/ml)
Comprehensive liver function panel (ALT, AST, total bilirubin, albumin, A/G ratio)
Abdominal color ultrasound (assess hepatic parenchymal echogenicity, surface smoothness, portal vein diameter, spleen thickness, and ascites)
Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (screening for high risk of liver cancer)
if_suspected: Transient hepatic elastography (FibroScan, to assess liver fibrosis stage F0-F4)
Contrast-enhanced MRI/CT of the upper abdomen (to determine benign or malignant nature when AFP is elevated or ultrasound reveals a liver nodule)
Liver biopsy for histopathologic examination (to assess inflammatory activity grade G and fibrosis stage S)
avoid: Blind frequent ordering of whole-body positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) in routine follow-up patients
Blind ERCP examination without indications of biliary obstruction

first_line: Potent, low-resistance nucleos(t)ide analogue antiviral therapy: first-line long-term standardized oral therapy with entecavir (ETV), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), or tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF)
Initiate immediately once indications are met (HBV DNA positive with persistently abnormal ALT, or with liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, or age >30 years with a family history)
Adjunctive hepatoprotective and anti-inflammatory therapy (bicyclol, glycyrrhizin preparations).
safety_warnings: Oral antiviral drugs must absolutely not be stopped arbitrarily on one's own! Unauthorized discontinuation can easily trigger viral rebound and fatal fulminant severe hepatitis
Regular monitoring of renal function and serum phosphorus is required with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) to prevent renal tubular injury and osteoporosis
Even if the virus becomes undetectable, chronic HBV-infected individuals remain at high risk for hepatocellular carcinoma and must undergo lifelong follow-up with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months
personalization: Women of childbearing age preparing for pregnancy and mother-to-child transmission prevention during pregnancy: choose tenofovir (TDF), which has good fetal safety
Patients with kidney disease or osteoporosis: preferentially use tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) or entecavir (ETV)
Patients with decompensated hepatitis B cirrhosis: antiviral therapy should be initiated immediately regardless of HBV DNA level

skills.presentation: Prodromal symptoms such as fever, headache, fatigue, and poor appetite, followed rapidly by a rash characterized by a 'centripetal distribution' (most abundant on the trunk and head, sparse on the distal extremities). The rash evolves in sequence from macules to papules to vesicles (typical 'teardrop' thin-walled clear blisters surrounded by erythema) to crusts, and lesions at different stages can be seen simultaneously in the same area ('four generations under one roof'), accompanied by marked pruritus.

first_questions: How many days have you had fever and rash on your body? Where on the body did the rash first appear?
Is the rash mainly concentrated on the scalp, chest, and back, with relatively few lesions on the hands and feet?
Are there small, sparkling blisters in the rash that look like dewdrops? Is it itchy?
followup_questions: In the 2-3 weeks before the rash appeared, was there anyone with chickenpox or herpes zoster at kindergarten, school, or around you?
Do you have erythematous macules, small papules, blisters, and crusts present at the same time on your body?
Do you have severe headache, drowsiness, vomiting, convulsions, or severe cough and shortness of breath? (to rule out varicella encephalitis and varicella pneumonia)
stop_conditions: The typical presentation of centripetal distribution, teardrop-like vesicles, and coexisting lesions at multiple stages has been confirmed
A clear epidemiological contact history has been obtained
Signs of varicella pneumonia, encephalitis, and secondary severe soft tissue bacterial infection have been strictly ruled out

essential: Infectious disease physical examination (whole-body rash morphology and distribution, and oral/scalp mucosal examination)
Complete blood count (total white blood cell count normal or low, with a relatively increased lymphocyte proportion)
if_suspected: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)-specific IgM antibody or PCR nucleic acid testing of vesicle fluid
Chest X-ray (for suspected varicella pneumonia with cough and dyspnea)
Head CT and lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (for suspected varicella encephalitis with neuropsychiatric symptoms)
avoid: Blind use of high-dose systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics for uncomplicated mild chickenpox
Incorrect use of systemic glucocorticoids because of misdiagnosis as an allergic rash (it can lead to disseminated varicella virus throughout the body and death)

first_line: Respiratory isolation (isolate until all rash lesions have completely crusted and fallen off)
Antiviral therapy: oral acyclovir (use within 24-48 hours of rash onset can significantly reduce severity), valacyclovir
Symptomatic antipruritic treatment: topical calamine lotion, oral antihistamines
For ruptured vesicles with secondary bacterial infection, topical mupirocin ointment
Strengthen skin care and trim fingernails to prevent scratching and infection.
safety_warnings: Systemic glucocorticoids are absolutely contraindicated during the acute phase of chickenpox (they can cause systemic viral dissemination, leading to severe hemorrhagic varicella or fatal multiple organ failure)
Aspirin is strictly prohibited for fever in children with chickenpox (it can easily induce fatal Reye syndrome); acetaminophen or ibuprofen is preferred for fever reduction
Chickenpox in adults of childbearing age and pregnant women is usually more severe than in children; early antiviral therapy and close monitoring for complications are needed
personalization: Immunocompromised or severe patients: give intravenous acyclovir as early as possible, with human varicella immunoglobulin if necessary

Pregnant women with chickenpox near delivery (from 5 days before delivery to within 2 days after delivery): neonates are highly susceptible to severe chickenpox; specific immunoglobulin should be injected immediately after birth and prophylactic antiviral therapy given
Close contacts: vaccination with live attenuated varicella vaccine within 72 hours after exposure can provide emergency post-exposure blocking protection

skills.presentation: Patients often present with prolonged fever of unknown origin, night sweats, and significant weight loss (more than 10% loss within 6 months). They are prone to recurrent oral candidiasis (thrush), herpes zoster, or herpes simplex. Persistent diarrhea, chronic cough with dyspnea, or purplish-red plaques resembling Kaposi sarcoma may appear on the skin. Some patients have generalized lymphadenopathy and symptoms of opportunistic infection.

first_questions: Have you ever had high-risk sexual behavior, intravenous drug use, or blood transfusion?
Have you recently had persistent fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss?
Have you had recurrent, difficult-to-heal oral ulcers, pneumonia, or skin rash?
followup_questions: If respiratory symptoms are present, ask further about tuberculosis contact history or hemoptysis.
If gastrointestinal symptoms are present, ask further about diarrhea frequency, character, and whether it is accompanied by abdominal pain.
If skin lesions are found, ask further about the color and morphological changes of the lesions and whether there is pain or itching.
stop_conditions: A clear history of high-risk exposure and typical symptoms of opportunistic infection have been established.
HIV antibody screening is positive and the epidemiological history has been collected.
Other common diseases have been excluded and the clinical presentation is highly suspected to be AIDS stage.

essential: HIV-1/2 antibody testing (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay)
HIV nucleic acid testing (viral load measurement)
CD4+ T lymphocyte count
Complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests
if_suspected: Chest CT (to rule out Pneumocystis pneumonia or tuberculosis)
Cerebrospinal fluid examination (to rule out cryptococcal meningitis or central nervous system lesions)
Stool culture and parasite examination (to identify the cause of chronic diarrhea)
Skin biopsy (to confirm Kaposi sarcoma)
avoid: Long-term use of broad-spectrum antibiotics without indications
Unnecessary invasive procedures (such as bone marrow puncture)
Use of high-dose antifungal drugs without assessing liver and kidney function

first_line: Immediately initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART); a three-drug regimen containing tenofovir (TDF/TAF) + lamivudine (3TC) + dolutegravir (DTG) is recommended. Treatment is lifelong and must not be stopped arbitrarily. At the same time, give prophylactic medication for opportunistic infections (such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for prevention of Pneumocystis pneumonia). Strengthen nutritional support, correct anemia and electrolyte disturbances, and provide psychological intervention and behavioral guidance.
safety_warnings: Stopping medication or missing doses without authorization is strictly prohibited to prevent the emergence of viral resistance.
Pay attention to drug-drug interactions, especially the concomitant use of rifampicin and protease inhibitors.
Be alert for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), and monitor for transient worsening of the disease after treatment.
personalization: Pregnant women should start ART in early pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child transmission, preferably with integrase inhibitors that have a high safety profile.
Patients with renal impairment should avoid tenofovir disoproxil fumarate; it can be changed to TAF or the dose adjusted.
Patients with comorbid tuberculosis should pay attention to metabolic conflicts between anti-tuberculosis drugs and ART drugs, and dosing times should be adjusted.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, and right upper quadrant discomfort or pain, with some having low-grade fever. Typical signs include jaundice (yellowing of the skin and sclera), hepatomegaly, and tenderness. About 30%-50% of patients develop dark urine resembling strong tea and pale stools. Symptoms usually appear 2-12 weeks after exposure; onset is relatively acute, and the condition is easily misdiagnosed as a cold or gastroenteritis.

first_questions: Have you recently had a blood transfusion, surgery, tattooing, puncture, or non-medical injection?
Have you been in contact with anyone known to be infected with hepatitis C virus, or shared personal items such as razors or toothbrushes?
In the two weeks before symptom onset, did you consume unclean food or alcohol?
followup_questions: If jaundice has occurred, please describe changes in urine color and stool characteristics.
Do you have a history of hepatitis B, HIV/AIDS, or any other chronic liver disease?
Have you recently taken any medications or supplements that may damage the liver?
stop_conditions: A recent high-risk exposure history is clearly established and typical hepatitis symptoms are present.
Laboratory tests show significantly elevated transaminases and positive anti-HCV.
Other common viral hepatitis (hepatitis A, B, and E) and drug-induced liver injury have been excluded.

essential: Hepatitis C virus antibody testing (Anti-HCV)
Quantitative hepatitis C virus nucleic acid testing (HCV-RNA)
Comprehensive liver function panel (ALT, AST, TBil, DBil, ALP, GGT)
if_suspected: Abdominal ultrasound (to assess liver morphology and biliary tract status)
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and E virus markers
Autoimmune liver disease antibody panel (to exclude autoimmune hepatitis)
avoid: Liver biopsy without indication (pathological confirmation is usually unnecessary in the acute phase)
Routine alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker screening (not first-line in the acute phase)
Repeated unnecessary contrast-enhanced imaging scans

first_line: Currently, early initiation of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy is recommended for acute hepatitis C, with a usual treatment course of 8-12 weeks. Preferred regimens include sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) once daily, or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (GLE/PIB) 3 times daily with food. During treatment, strict alcohol abstinence is required, hepatotoxic drugs should be avoided, and bed rest is recommended until symptoms resolve. Most patients can achieve a sustained virologic response (SVR) with standard treatment and attain clinical cure.
safety_warnings: Coadministration of sofosbuvir with amiodarone is strictly prohibited, as it may cause severe bradycardia and even death.
Protease inhibitor-containing regimens are contraindicated in patients with decompensated cirrhosis.
Liver function should be monitored during treatment, and vigilance is needed for worsening drug-induced liver injury.
personalization: In patients with renal impairment, doses of some DAA drugs should be adjusted according to creatinine clearance, or alternative regimens should be selected.
DAA use should be cautious in pregnant and breastfeeding women; benefits and risks should be weighed and a specialist consulted.
In patients with HIV coinfection, drug interactions should be assessed and a combined treatment plan developed.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with sudden onset of fatigue, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, with dark yellow urine resembling strong tea. Some develop fever and vague right upper quadrant pain. Signs may include jaundice of the skin and sclera, and hepatomegaly with tenderness. It is more common in middle-aged men or pregnant women, and there is a history of consumption of undercooked pork/seafood or travel to endemic areas. Symptoms worsen during the icteric phase, but systemic toxemic symptoms are relatively mild, and the course is usually self-limited.

first_questions: Have you recently eaten undercooked meat (especially pork liver) or drunk unboiled water?
Have you noticed dark urine, yellowing of the whites of the eyes, or marked fatigue?
Do you have a history of chronic liver disease or an immunosuppressed state?
followup_questions: If you are a woman of childbearing age, when was your last menstrual period, and are you pregnant?
If your symptoms continue to worsen, have you had confusion or any bleeding tendency?
In the 1-2 months before symptom onset, did you travel to or live in an endemic area, or have contact with anyone with similar symptoms?
stop_conditions: Typical symptoms are clear and the epidemiological history is clear, allowing a preliminary diagnosis.
Laboratory tests have confirmed positive anti-HEV IgM.
There are no warning signs of severe disease (such as coagulopathy or hepatic encephalopathy).

essential: Serum anti-HEV IgM antibody testing
Comprehensive liver function panel (ALT, AST, TBil, DBil)
Coagulation profile (PT, INR)
if_suspected: Abdominal ultrasound (to assess liver morphology and biliary tract status)
Screening for viral hepatitis markers such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV
Complete blood count (to assess changes in white blood cells and platelets)
avoid: Liver biopsy (unless the diagnosis is unclear or overlapping infection is suspected)
Routine non-contrast CT (not first-line; used only to exclude space-occupying lesions)
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (in the absence of evidence of bacterial infection)

first_line: Supportive care and symptomatic treatment are the mainstays. Bed rest and a high-calorie, easily digestible diet should be provided. Hepatoprotective and enzyme-lowering drugs (such as polyene phosphatidylcholine or glycyrrhizin preparations) are used for 2-4 weeks until indicators return to normal. Hepatotoxic drugs should be avoided. Severe cases require close monitoring and, if necessary, artificial liver support.
safety_warnings: Potential hepatotoxic drugs such as acetaminophen are strictly prohibited
Be alert for delayed viral clearance when used with immunosuppressants
Pregnant women with infection require prevention of fulminant hepatitis risk and prompt referral
personalization: Older adults and patients with underlying liver disease require a prolonged observation period to prevent liver failure
Immunocompromised patients (e.g., organ transplant recipients) may require prolonged antiviral observation or consideration of ribavirin (with side effects weighed)
Ribavirin is contraindicated in pregnant women; intensified monitoring is required and termination of pregnancy should be considered at the appropriate time

skills.presentation: Patients often report redness, swelling, heat, and pain in the regional lymph node area; on palpation, the lymph nodes are enlarged and relatively firm, with tenderness. Some patients may have systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue. Lesions most often occur in the neck, axilla, or groin, and are common in children and adolescents.

first_questions: Have you recently had any skin breakdown or infection?
Is the pain accompanied by fever or other systemic discomfort?
followup_questions: If the pain worsens, does it affect your daily activities?
Have you recently had contact with anyone with an infectious disease?
stop_conditions: Local redness, swelling, heat, pain, and associated symptoms are clearly defined
The patient has no history of other systemic diseases
Initial examination suggests typical findings

essential: Complete blood count
Ultrasound examination
C-reactive protein testing
if_suspected: Bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Tuberculin skin test
Imaging studies (e.g., CT)
avoid: Unnecessary radiological examinations
Nonspecific immunological tests

first_line: First-line treatment includes antibiotics (such as cephalosporins or penicillins), with the dose adjusted according to body weight, usually for 7-10 days. Local warm compresses are also recommended to relieve symptoms. If an abscess forms, incision and drainage are required.
safety_warnings: Related drugs are contraindicated in patients allergic to penicillin
Monitor for abnormal liver and kidney function
Avoid long-term use of broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent resistance
personalization: Doses for children should be calculated precisely by body weight
Attention should be paid to drug metabolism capacity in older adults
Certain antibiotics should be used cautiously in pregnant women, and safe alternatives should be selected

skills.presentation: Patients often report an insidious onset of vague or dull right lower quadrant pain, accompanied by tenesmus. The typical manifestation is jam-like, foul-smelling, bloody mucopurulent stools, several to more than ten times per day, without marked systemic toxemic symptoms such as high fever and chills. Some patients may have nausea, abdominal bloating, and mild fever. If the liver is involved, pain and tenderness in the liver region may occur.

first_questions: Have you recently had a history of unclean food consumption or travel to endemic areas (tropical/subtropical)?
Are your stools dark red and jam-like with a peculiar foul odor?
In which abdominal region is the pain mainly located, and is it accompanied by tenesmus?
followup_questions: If you have pain in the liver region, does it tend to worsen at night, and is there any radiating pain?
If the course is prolonged, have you had weight loss or recurrent chronic diarrhea?
Have you recently taken antibiotics or antidiarrheal drugs, so that drug interference can be excluded?
stop_conditions: When typical jam-like stools and a history of endemic area contact have been clearly described, and the signs are consistent.
When stool microscopy has been completed and Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites or cysts are found.
When the patient's vital signs are stable and there are no signs of acute perforation or massive hemorrhage.

essential: Routine stool examination (microscopic search for Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites or cysts)
Colonoscopy (to observe the morphology of intestinal mucosal ulcers and obtain biopsies)
Serological antibody testing (for invasive cases)
if_suspected: Abdominal ultrasound or CT (to evaluate extraintestinal complications such as amebic liver abscess)
Complete blood count (to assess anemia severity and changes in white blood cells)
Liver function tests (to assess liver involvement)
avoid: Blind use of potent antidiarrheal drugs (may induce toxic megacolon)
Unnecessary barium enema (increases the risk of intestinal perforation)
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (avoid masking the condition before diagnosis is confirmed)

first_line: First-line treatment is metronidazole (0.4-0.8g, 3 times daily, for 7-10 days) to eradicate tissue trophozoites, followed by an intraluminal amebicide such as diloxanide or paromomycin to clear intestinal cysts and prevent relapse. Severe cases require intravenous administration. At the same time, attention should be paid to fluid replacement to correct electrolyte disturbances, and nutritional support should be provided when necessary.
safety_warnings: Alcohol consumption is strictly prohibited during metronidazole treatment and for 3 days after discontinuation to prevent disulfiram-like reactions
Use with caution in pregnant women (especially in early pregnancy) and breastfeeding women; benefits and risks should be weighed
Common adverse reactions include metallic taste, nausea and vomiting, and neurological symptoms, which require monitoring
personalization: In children, doses should be calculated precisely by body weight to avoid neurotoxicity from overdose
In patients with hepatic impairment, the metronidazole dose should be adjusted and liver enzymes closely monitored
Immunosuppressed patients require a prolonged treatment course and combination of multiple drugs to prevent relapse

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of sudden-onset high fever (>38.5℃) and chills, accompanied by local redness, swelling, heat, and pain or dysfunction of specific organs. For example, respiratory manifestations include purulent sputum and chest pain; urinary manifestations include urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria; gastrointestinal manifestations include diarrhea with mucopurulent bloody stools. Some severe patients may develop systemic toxemic symptoms such as confusion and hypotension; the source and severity of infection need to be rapidly identified in conjunction with the medical history.

first_questions: How long has the fever lasted? What was the highest body temperature?
Where do you feel the most discomfort right now? Is there any abnormal discharge?
Have you recently had trauma, surgery, or contact with patients with infectious diseases?
followup_questions: If you have difficulty breathing, have you had shortness of breath or cyanosis?
If you have abdominal pain and diarrhea, what is the stool like? Is there tenesmus?
Do you have any underlying diseases (such as diabetes) or an immunosuppressed state?
stop_conditions: The site of infection, typical symptoms, and high-risk factors have been identified, and vital signs are stable.
The patient has received empiric antibiotic therapy and has shown no worsening after 24 hours of observation.
Key laboratory test results (such as complete blood count and cultures) have been returned and have guided medication use.

essential: Complete blood count (white blood cell count and neutrophil percentage)
C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT)
Pathogen cultures (blood/urine/sputum/secretions culture + antimicrobial susceptibility testing)
if_suspected: Imaging studies (chest CT, abdominal ultrasound, or MRI)
Blood gas analysis (to assess hypoxia and acid-base balance)
Liver and kidney function and electrolyte testing
avoid: Blind use of broad-spectrum antibiotics before specimen collection, leading to negative cultures
Repeated testing of nonspecific inflammatory markers without indication
Invasive procedures (such as lumbar puncture) in mild cases

first_line: Select susceptible antibiotics empirically according to the site of infection and local resistance patterns (such as cephalosporins and penicillins), then adjust according to susceptibility results. Oral therapy for mild cases and intravenous infusion for severe cases. The course is usually 7-14 days, depending on the condition. At the same time, provide nonpharmacologic supportive treatment such as fluid replacement and fever reduction, and maintain water and electrolyte balance.
safety_warnings: Antibiotics should be strictly avoided in patients allergic to β-lactam drugs
Pay attention to interactions between macrolides and antiarrhythmic drugs to prevent QT interval prolongation
Be alert to the nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity of aminoglycosides; serum drug concentrations need monitoring
personalization: Older adults require dose reduction and close monitoring of renal function to prevent drug accumulation
Tetracyclines and quinolones are contraindicated in pregnant women; penicillins or cephalosporins are preferred
Avoid quinolones in children to prevent cartilage damage; calculate doses by body weight

skills.presentation: Patients often have a clear history of being scratched or bitten by a cat (especially a kitten), with an incubation period of about 1-2 weeks. Typical manifestations are erythema, papules, or pustules on the local skin, followed by regional lymph node enlargement, pain, and tenderness, most commonly in the axilla, neck, or groin. Low-grade fever, fatigue, headache, and other systemic symptoms are often present. Some patients may develop conjunctival hyperemia or ocular granulomas.

first_questions: Have you recently been scratched or bitten by a cat, or had a cat lick broken skin?
Has the injured area developed redness, swelling, induration, or purulent discharge?
Have you recently had fever, fatigue, or unexplained lymph node enlargement?
followup_questions: If your lymph nodes are noticeably enlarged: Is the lump severely tender? How mobile is it? Has it ulcerated or drained pus?
If you have eye symptoms: Has your vision decreased? Do you have photophobia or tearing?
Have you had HIV infection, an organ transplant, or long-term use of steroids/immunosuppressants?
stop_conditions: A history of cat scratch has been confirmed and typical local lymphadenitis manifestations are present
Necessary physical examination has been completed and other serious sources of infection have been excluded
The patient has no high-risk immunodeficiency background and symptoms are mild and stable

essential: Complete blood count and C-reactive protein testing
Bartonella serologic antibody testing (IgM/IgG)
Ultrasound of the affected lymph nodes
if_suspected: Lymph node needle biopsy (for confirmation and to exclude lymphoma and tuberculosis)
PCR testing for Bartonella DNA in blood or tissue samples
Fundoscopy (when endophthalmitis is suspected)
avoid: Blind culturing before routine empirical long-term antibiotic therapy
Unnecessary CT/MRI scans (unless deep abscess or complications are suspected)
Incision and drainage for simple superficial lymphadenitis

first_line: Most mild cases resolve spontaneously and require no specific treatment. For symptomatic patients, oral azithromycin is preferred (adults 500mg on the first day, then 250mg/day for the next 3 days

children dosed by weight), course 5-7 days. For severe cases or immunosuppressed patients, rifampicin combined with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole may be selected, course 2-4 weeks. Combine with local hot compresses to relieve lymph node swelling and pain; avoid squeezing.
safety_warnings: Rifampicin is a strong hepatic enzyme inducer; liver function should be monitored and drug interactions should be watched for
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole may cause rash, bone marrow suppression, and hyperkalemia; use with caution in patients with an allergic predisposition
Azithromycin may prolong the QT interval; patients with heart disease require ECG assessment
personalization: Azithromycin is preferred for pregnant and breastfeeding women; avoid tetracyclines and quinolones
Doses in children must be strictly adjusted by body weight; avoid aspirin for fever reduction
Immunodeficient patients require a prolonged course and close follow-up, with combined intravenous therapy when necessary

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of increased urethral or cervical discharge, which is mucopurulent, accompanied by urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, and other voiding discomfort. Women may have lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, or irregular vaginal bleeding; men may have redness and swelling of the urethral meatus and a small amount of thin discharge. Some patients have insidious symptoms found only during physical examination, but vigilance is needed for complications such as persistent pain caused by epididymitis or pelvic inflammatory disease.

first_questions: Have you recently had unsafe sex or a new partner?
Do you have urethral stinging, abnormal discharge, or lower abdominal pain?
followup_questions: How long have the symptoms lasted, and have they resolved on their own?
Do you have a history of similar infections or a family history of sexually transmitted diseases?
stop_conditions: A history of high-risk sexual behavior has been confirmed and typical symptoms (discharge, dysuria) have been present for more than 3 days
The patient has provided recent nucleic acid test results and the diagnosis has been confirmed
Symptoms are mild with no signs of complications, and an initial screening plan has been formulated

essential: Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) of urine or swab samples
Genitourinary physical examination (inspect discharge and tenderness)
if_suspected: Gonococcal smear and culture (to identify coinfection)
Pelvic ultrasound (to assess the adnexa when pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected)
Syphilis and HIV serologic screening (routine comorbidity screening)
avoid: Gram stain microscopy alone (low diagnostic value for Chlamydia)
Failure to perform pathogen testing before empiric use of broad-spectrum antibiotics
Unnecessary invasive surgical exploration

first_line: First-line doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 7 consecutive days

If pregnant or allergic to tetracyclines, switch to azithromycin 1g as a single oral dose. Strictly abstain from alcohol during treatment, and avoid sexual intercourse until symptoms resolve and the course is completed. Treat sexual partners at the same time to prevent reinfection. Nonpharmacologic interventions include maintaining local hygiene and regular follow-up.
safety_warnings: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnant women and children under 8 years of age and may cause photosensitivity reactions
Azithromycin may prolong the QT interval; use with caution in patients with heart disease
If severe rash or difficulty breathing occurs during treatment, stop the drug immediately and seek medical care
personalization: Azithromycin is preferred in pregnant women; avoid doxycycline because of effects on fetal skeletal development
Patients with hepatic or renal impairment require dose adjustment or a prolonged dosing interval
For patients with poor adherence, consider a single high-dose regimen or transition to intravenous administration

skills.presentation: Patients often present with dull right upper abdominal pain, abdominal bloating, indigestion, and fatigue, and some have mild fever or urticaria. Typical symptoms include epigastric discomfort, diarrhea, or nausea after eating raw fish. Severe cases may develop biliary colic, jaundice, or hepatosplenomegaly. If left untreated for a long time, it may progress to cholangitis, gallstones, or even cholangiocarcinoma; unexplained abnormal liver function warrants vigilance.

first_questions: Have you recently eaten sashimi, drunken shrimp, or undercooked freshwater fish?
Have you had right upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, or itching of the skin?
Do you have a history of similar symptoms or hepatobiliary disease?
followup_questions: Is the abdominal pain related to eating greasy food?
Have you had fever, chills, or darkening of the urine (jaundice)?
Is there a similar case in your family or a history of shared food consumption?
stop_conditions: A history of eating raw freshwater fish is clear and typical gastrointestinal symptoms are present
Ova have been detected in stool or serology is positive
Other hepatobiliary diseases have been excluded and the diagnostic evidence is sufficient

essential: Routine stool examination (to look for ova)
Complete blood count (eosinophil count)
Hepatobiliary ultrasound
if_suspected: Specific serologic antibody testing (ELISA)
CT or MRI (to assess biliary dilation or mass lesions)
ERCP (when bile duct obstruction is suspected)
avoid: Invasive cholangiography without indication
Nontargeted broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Unnecessary liver needle biopsy

first_line: First-line praziquantel, adult dose 25mg/kg three times daily for 2 consecutive days

or 75mg/kg as a single oral dose. For mild cases, cholagogue drugs may be used to relieve symptoms. During treatment, a light diet is recommended, and avoid eating raw food again. Recheck stool for ova 2-4 weeks after completing the course to assess efficacy.
safety_warnings: Use with caution in patients with epilepsy; it may lower the seizure threshold
Patients with severe cardiac, hepatic, or renal impairment require dose reduction and monitoring
Dizziness, abdominal pain, and other reactions may occur after taking the drug and require observation
personalization: Calculate doses precisely by body weight in children to avoid overdose
In pregnant women, use only when the condition is severe after weighing the benefits and risks
Pay attention to cardiovascular monitoring in older patients

skills.presentation: Patients often present with acute influenza-like symptoms, including fever, dry cough, chest pain, fatigue, and arthralgia (especially of the ankles and knees). Some patients develop a characteristic red nodular rash (erythema nodosum) or purpura. If the disease progresses to a chronic or disseminated form, persistent cough, weight loss, night sweats, and even skin ulcers, osteoarticular destruction, or meningeal symptoms may occur.

first_questions: Have you recently traveled to endemic areas such as the southwestern United States, Mexico, or Central America?
Are your symptoms accompanied by joint pain in specific areas or a skin rash?
followup_questions: If you have joint pain, which specific joints are affected? Is it accompanied by redness and swelling?
Do you have difficulty breathing, persistent high fever, or neurological abnormalities (such as headache or neck stiffness)?
stop_conditions: A clear epidemiological history has been established and typical symptoms (influenza-like symptoms plus erythema nodosum) are all present.
Other common respiratory infections have been excluded and there are no signs of high-risk dissemination.
The patient's symptoms are mild and there is no background of immunosuppression, suggesting a self-limited condition.

essential: Serological testing: complement fixation (CF), immunodiffusion (ID)
Chest X-ray or CT
Complete blood count (CBC) and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP)
if_suspected: Fungal culture (sputum, blood, or tissue specimens)
Cerebrospinal fluid examination (when central nervous system involvement is suspected)
Skin biopsy or histopathological examination (for skin lesions)
avoid: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (unless there is evidence of bacterial coinfection)
Unnecessary invasive procedures (such as bronchoscopy) without a clear indication
Diagnosing solely on clinical symptoms while ignoring epidemiological history

first_line: Asymptomatic or mild primary infection usually does not require antifungal therapy, and supportive care is the mainstay. For moderate-to-severe or persistent symptoms, oral fluconazole (400-800 mg/day) or itraconazole (200-400 mg/day) is preferred, for at least 3-6 months. Severe disseminated infection requires intravenous amphotericin B induction therapy, followed by oral azole maintenance.
safety_warnings: Azoles may cause hepatotoxicity, and liver function should be monitored regularly.
Avoid concomitant use with warfarin, statins, or certain antiarrhythmic drugs to prevent interactions.
Amphotericin B may cause nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances, and renal function and potassium and magnesium levels should be closely monitored.
personalization: In pregnant women, amphotericin B is preferred, and azoles should be avoided.
Immunocompromised patients (such as those with HIV/AIDS) require prolonged treatment and consideration of combination therapy.
In elderly patients, drug doses should be adjusted according to renal function.

skills.presentation: Affected infants often present with microcephaly, ocular abnormalities such as cataracts or glaucoma, and cardiac murmurs (such as patent ductus arteriosus) present at birth. Some infants have hearing loss, hepatosplenomegaly, rash ('blueberry muffin' appearance), and intracranial calcifications. The classic features are the 'triad': deafness, eye disease, and heart disease. If the mother has a history of fever or rash during pregnancy, this disease should be highly suspected.

first_questions: Did the mother have fever, rash, or cold-like symptoms during early pregnancy?
After birth, was the newborn found to have visual impairment, hearing abnormalities, or a cardiac murmur?
Is there a family history of similar congenital defects?
followup_questions: If the mother had a rash, at exactly what gestational week did it occur?
What were the newborn hearing screening results? Has sensorineural hearing loss been confirmed?
Did echocardiography show specific structural abnormalities (such as pulmonary artery stenosis)?
stop_conditions: A history of maternal infection during pregnancy has been established, and the newborn has the typical triad manifestations.
Laboratory testing has confirmed evidence of intrauterine rubella virus infection in the fetus.
Key imaging examinations have been completed and other teratogenic factors have been excluded.

essential: Serological testing: specific IgM antibody and IgG antibody titers
Urine and saliva PCR testing: rubella virus nucleic acid
Ophthalmology and otolaryngology specialist evaluation: slit-lamp examination and auditory evoked potential testing
if_suspected: Brain MRI or CT: to screen for intracranial calcifications and brain developmental abnormalities
Echocardiography: to assess the type and severity of congenital heart disease
Liver function tests and complete blood count: to assess hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (since this is not caused by bacterial infection)
Whole-body PET-CT without indication
Repeated unnecessary invasive puncture procedures

first_line: There is currently no specific antiviral drug, and treatment is mainly symptomatic and supportive. The focus is multidisciplinary collaborative management: surgical correction for cataracts; early hearing aid fitting or cochlear implantation for hearing impairment; and elective surgery for cardiac malformations according to severity. At the same time, nutritional support should be strengthened, secondary infections prevented, and long-term rehabilitation training and psychological intervention provided.
safety_warnings: The use of unproven immunomodulators or pulse steroid therapy is strictly prohibited.
Avoid ototoxic drugs to prevent worsening of hearing damage.
Consider the burden of drug metabolism, and adjust doses in patients with hepatic or renal impairment.
personalization: In premature infants, nutritional regimens and anti-infective strategies need to be adjusted.
For those with severe heart disease, a perioperative management plan should be developed jointly with cardiology.
Children with hearing impairment should start speech rehabilitation training as early as possible to meet their special needs.

skills.presentation: Patients often report seizures of unknown cause, manifesting as sudden loss of consciousness and limb convulsions. Some patients may have palpable painless subcutaneous nodules or symptoms of increased intracranial pressure such as headache and vomiting. If the eyes are involved, they may report blurred vision or floaters; if muscles are involved, there may be aching and weakness. The severity of symptoms depends on the location and number of cysticerci and the host immune response.

first_questions: Have you ever eaten raw pork or had contact with pig feces?
Have you had recurrent convulsions or loss of consciousness?
Have you ever felt small hard nodules on your skin?
followup_questions: Is the headache accompanied by projectile vomiting?
Is the visual decline related to eye movement?
Have you recently had significant weight loss or fever?
stop_conditions: A clear history of raw food consumption has been established, and typical epilepsy or subcutaneous nodules are present.
Imaging has indicated cystic lesions in the brain.
Serological antibody testing is strongly positive.

essential: Non-contrast head CT
Contrast-enhanced head MRI
Serum cysticercus antibody ELISA
if_suspected: Fundoscopy
Whole-body muscle ultrasound
Lumbar puncture with pressure measurement and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
avoid: Routine chest X-ray (unless concurrent tuberculosis is suspected)
Whole-body PET-CT without indication
Unnecessary invasive biopsy

first_line: Oral albendazole is preferred, at a dose of 15 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 7-14 days, repeated if necessary. Dexamethasone is used concomitantly to prevent inflammatory reactions. For patients with intracranial hypertension, reduce intracranial pressure first before antihelminthic treatment. Severe cases require hospitalization and monitoring, with antiepileptic drugs to control seizures.
safety_warnings: It is strictly contraindicated in women in early pregnancy and during breastfeeding.
Concomitant use with cimetidine may increase plasma drug concentrations and cause toxicity.
During the initial treatment period, it may easily induce cerebral edema or worsening of epilepsy, requiring close monitoring.
personalization: In children, calculate the dose precisely by body weight and monitor liver function.
In patients with hepatic or renal impairment, reduce the dose and prolong the dosing interval.
For patients with frequent seizures, antiepileptic treatment should be intensified simultaneously.

skills.presentation: Immunocompetent individuals are often asymptomatic or present with an infectious mononucleosis-like syndrome, such as fever, sore throat, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy. Immunosuppressed patients (such as transplant recipients or those with HIV/AIDS) may develop pneumonia (dry cough, dyspnea), retinitis (blurred vision, visual field defects), colitis (abdominal pain, diarrhea), or encephalitis (disturbed consciousness, convulsions). Neonatal infection may manifest as jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, and hearing loss.

first_questions: Have you recently had fever, fatigue, or cold-like symptoms?
Are you currently receiving immunosuppressive treatment (such as post-organ transplant medications or chemotherapy), or do you have a history of HIV infection?
Have you experienced blurred vision, dark shadows obscuring your vision, or hearing loss?
followup_questions: If you have respiratory symptoms, please describe whether there is a persistent dry cough or shortness of breath.
If you have eye discomfort, is it accompanied by eye pain or flashes of light?
Have you recently had unexplained abnormal liver function or rash?
stop_conditions: The patient's immune status and typical target-organ involvement symptoms (such as pneumonia or retinitis) have been clarified.
It has been confirmed that there are no high-risk factors and symptoms are mild, suggesting a self-limited infection.
Key history (medication history, underlying diseases) and physical signs have been fully collected, sufficient to guide initial testing.

essential: Serum CMV IgM/IgG antibody testing
Quantitative CMV DNA PCR (blood or body fluids)
Complete blood count and liver function tests
if_suspected: Fundus fluorescein angiography or OCT (when retinitis is suspected)
High-resolution chest CT (when interstitial pneumonia is suspected)
Cerebrospinal fluid CMV PCR and MRI (when central nervous system infection is suspected)
avoid: Diagnosing acute infection based solely on positive IgG (IgM or PCR should be incorporated)
Invasive tissue biopsy in asymptomatic immunocompetent individuals
Blind use of antiviral drugs before excluding other pathogens

first_line: For symptomatic immunosuppressed patients, intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 14-21 days) is preferred, and after the condition stabilizes, treatment may be switched to oral valganciclovir. For mild cases or prophylactic treatment, oral valganciclovir may be used. Non-pharmacological interventions include supportive care and, when necessary, adjustment of immunosuppressant doses. During treatment, blood counts should be closely monitored to prevent bone marrow suppression.
safety_warnings: It is contraindicated in pregnant women (risk of teratogenicity), and strict contraception is required during the reproductive years.
Concomitant use with bone marrow-suppressive drugs (such as zidovudine or azathioprine) is strictly prohibited to prevent severe agranulocytosis.
Renal impairment should be closely monitored; before administration, creatinine clearance must be assessed and the dose adjusted.
personalization: In patients with renal impairment, the dose must be significantly reduced according to creatinine clearance.
In elderly patients, the starting dose should be conservative, and neutrophil counts should be closely monitored.
Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients require prolonged treatment until the viral load remains persistently negative.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with sudden high fever, accompanied by severe headache (especially retro-orbital pain), generalized myalgia and arthralgia ('break-bone pain'), and some develop rash, nausea, and vomiting. The typical presentation is biphasic fever or persistent high fever for 3-5 days followed by rash during the defervescence phase. Be alert for bleeding tendency such as gum bleeding, epistaxis, or skin ecchymoses, and for warning signs of shock such as abdominal pain and restlessness.

first_questions: In the 14 days before illness onset, have you had any mosquito bites or traveled to an epidemic area?
Have you had sudden high fever, retro-orbital pain, or severe generalized muscle and joint pain?
followup_questions: If you have a rash or bleeding spots, where are they located, and have you had gum or nasal bleeding?
If your temperature has fallen but your symptoms are worsening, have you had severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or changes in consciousness?
stop_conditions: Epidemiologic history is clear and the classic triad of fever, pain, and rash is present
Marked thrombocytopenia with bleeding manifestations
Early signs of shock (e.g., cold clammy extremities, rapid pulse) are present

essential: Complete blood count (with particular attention to leukopenia and thrombocytopenia)
Dengue NS1 antigen testing or IgM/IgG antibody testing
Coagulation profile
if_suspected: Liver function tests (to assess elevated transaminases)
Hematocrit measurement (to monitor hemoconcentration)
Chest X-ray (to evaluate for pleural effusion)
avoid: Routine use of aspirin or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as diagnostic agents before antipyretic measures
Invasive procedures without an indication, such as bone marrow aspiration

first_line: There is currently no specific antiviral drug; management is primarily symptomatic and supportive. The first priority is adequate fluid replacement to maintain water and electrolyte balance, choosing oral or intravenous fluids according to the degree of dehydration. For fever, acetaminophen is the first choice; aspirin or ibuprofen are strictly prohibited to prevent bleeding risk. Closely monitor vital signs and platelet changes; severe cases should be promptly transferred to the ICU for interventions such as fluid resuscitation and plasma exchange.
safety_warnings: Absolute contraindication to aspirin, ibuprofen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to avoid provoking severe bleeding
Avoid overhydration leading to pulmonary edema; hematocrit should be monitored dynamically
Be alert for sepsis caused by secondary bacterial infection
personalization: In pediatric patients, fluid volume must be calculated strictly to prevent volume overload
In pregnant women and older adults, lower the threshold for fluid infusion rate and strengthen monitoring of cardiac and renal function
Use acetaminophen with caution in patients with underlying liver disease and adjust the dose

skills.presentation: Patients often present with sudden high fever, accompanied by severe headache, generalized myalgia, and rash. The typical presentation is a pink maculopapular rash appearing on days 5-7 after illness onset, usually starting on the trunk and spreading to the extremities, but the palms and soles are usually spared. Some patients may have nausea, vomiting, cough, or mild hepatosplenomegaly. Symptoms resemble influenza but are more severe, and the characteristic rash is key to recognition.

first_questions: Have you recently had contact with rats or their excreta?
When did the fever and rash start?
Are they accompanied by severe headache or muscle pain?
followup_questions: If you have had contact with rodents, what was the type of contact and when did it occur?
If you have a rash, did it start on the trunk and spread to the extremities?
If you have neurologic symptoms, have you had changes in consciousness or seizures?
stop_conditions: Fever, rash, and a history of rodent contact have been clearly established
Initial physical examination has been completed and typical signs have been found
Laboratory test results support the diagnosis

essential: Weil-Felix test
Serologic testing (e.g., IgM antibody testing)
Complete blood count
if_suspected: Liver function tests
Cerebrospinal fluid examination (if neurologic symptoms are present)
Chest X-ray (to rule out pulmonary complications)
avoid: Unnecessary empiric trial of antibiotics
Invasive procedures without an indication, such as bone marrow aspiration

first_line: First-line treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7-10 days. Severe cases may receive intravenous administration. Nonpharmacologic interventions include adequate fluid replacement, fever control, and rest. Early treatment can significantly reduce mortality.
safety_warnings: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnant women; an alternative regimen should be used
Avoid concomitant use with calcium-, magnesium-, or aluminum-containing antacids to prevent impaired absorption
Monitor for allergic reactions and gastrointestinal discomfort
personalization: In children, adjust the dose by body weight, usually 2.2 mg/kg per dose
In older adults, adjust the dose according to renal function
Immunosuppressed patients may require a prolonged course

skills.presentation: Patients have persistent or recurrent fever for more than 3 weeks, with temperature fluctuating above 38.3℃, and the cause remains unclear after initial outpatient evaluation (e.g., complete blood count, chest X-ray) and 3 days of inpatient observation. It is often accompanied by nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss, but there is no clear localized source of infection or typical rash.

first_questions: How long has the fever lasted? What is the highest temperature? Is there any pattern?
Have you recently traveled to or lived in an epidemic area, had contact with animals, or eaten contaminated food?
Do you have accompanying symptoms such as joint pain, rash, cough, or abdominal pain?
followup_questions: If you have joint pain, please specify the location and whether you have morning stiffness.
If you have a rash, please describe its appearance and distribution.
If you have recent travel history, please specify the exact locations and duration of stay.
If you have used antibiotics, please provide the specific drug name and the effect on fever.
stop_conditions: The fever curve, medication history, and history of underlying diseases have been recorded in detail.
The epidemiologic history has been completed and there is no high-risk exposure.
The patient's vital signs are stable, with no indication for emergency resuscitation.

essential: Blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic)
Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, PCT)
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and chest
if_suspected: Autoantibody panel and quantitative immunoglobulins
Bone marrow aspiration smear and biopsy
Whole-body PET-CT scan
avoid: Blind repeated plain chest X-rays
Empiric combination use of broad-spectrum antibiotics without an indication
Unnecessary invasive organ biopsy

first_line: Before the cause is identified, routine use of antibiotics or corticosteroids is generally not recommended. For high fever (>39℃), physical cooling or acetaminophen may be used for fever control. If an occult infection is highly suspected, targeted anti-infective therapy should be given after etiologic evidence supports it.
If an autoimmune disease is considered, low-dose glucocorticoid therapy may be used after diagnosis is confirmed. At the same time, strengthen nutritional support and fluid management.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of glucocorticoids without an indication, which may mask the condition
Be aware of gastrointestinal injury and hepatic and renal impairment caused by antipyretics and analgesics
Be alert for dysbiosis and emergence of resistant bacteria caused by antibiotic misuse
personalization: Use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with caution in older adults to prevent kidney injury
In pregnant women, acetaminophen is the first choice; tetracyclines and quinolones are contraindicated
In children, calculate antipyretic doses strictly to prevent seizures

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent watery diarrhea, with foul-smelling, greasy stools, accompanied by marked abdominal bloating, abdominal cramps, and frequent belching. Symptoms usually appear 1-2 weeks after drinking contaminated water or contact with contaminated water bodies, and may be accompanied by fatigue, nausea, and weight loss. Some patients present with alternating intermittent diarrhea and constipation, and children may have growth retardation.

first_questions: Have you recently drunk untreated water, camped outdoors, or traveled?
Is the diarrhea accompanied by foul-smelling greasy stools and severe abdominal bloating?
How long have the symptoms lasted, and have you had significant weight loss?
followup_questions: If you mention raw food or unboiled water, please specify when and how often you consumed it.
If you describe fatty diarrhea, please say whether the stool floats on water or is difficult to flush away.
If symptoms are prolonged, please tell us whether you have an underlying immunodeficiency or a history of biliary disease.
stop_conditions: A recent history of drinking contaminated water or exposure to contaminated water is clear and typical steatorrhea symptoms have lasted more than 1 week
Key epidemiologic history has been collected and other triggers of acute gastroenteritis have been excluded
The patient has provided sufficient information pointing to parasitic infection, and no further questioning about unrelated history is needed.

essential: Stool routine examination (including occult blood)
Stool antigen testing (Giardia lamblia antigen)
Stool smear for cysts or trophozoites
if_suspected: Small intestinal biopsy (for refractory or difficult-to-diagnose cases)
Complete blood count and electrolytes (to assess the degree of dehydration and malnutrition)
Liver function tests (to evaluate for concomitant biliary infection)
avoid: Blind use of empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics
Noncontrast abdominal CT without an indication (unless a complication such as intestinal obstruction is suspected)
Repeated low-sensitivity routine microscopy without antigen test support

first_line: First-line treatment is metronidazole; the adult dose is usually 250 mg orally three times daily for 5-7 days

Or tinidazole 2 g as a single dose. Probiotics are also recommended to regulate intestinal flora, and patients with severe dehydration require fluid replacement to correct electrolyte disturbances. Avoid alcohol during treatment to prevent a disulfiram-like reaction.
safety_warnings: Metronidazole is contraindicated in pregnant women (especially in early pregnancy) and breastfeeding women; the risks and benefits must be weighed
Strictly prohibit alcohol consumption during use; otherwise it can cause a severe disulfiram-like reaction
It may cause nausea, a metallic taste, and headache; patients should be told these are common adverse reactions
personalization: In children, calculate the dose by body weight (usually 15-20 mg/kg/day in divided doses), with the same course duration as adults
In patients with hepatic or renal impairment, reduce the dose or extend the dosing interval and closely monitor liver function
In immunosuppressed patients with poor response, consider combination therapy or extending the course to 14 days

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe sore throat and dysphagia, accompanied by fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. Some patients have mild or no symptoms and are easily misdiagnosed as ordinary tonsillitis. Typical signs include pharyngeal erythema, yellow-white purulent exudate on the tonsillar surface, and occasionally ulcers. If accompanied by a history of oral sex and the above symptoms, this disease should be highly suspected.

first_questions: Have you had unprotected oral sex recently?
What is the exact duration of your sore throat and fever?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or painful swelling of the cervical lymph nodes?
followup_questions: If the sore throat is severe and there is purulent exudate, ask further: 'Is the exudate yellow-white?'
If symptoms are mild, ask further: 'Have you had recent exposure to other sexually transmitted infections?'
If you have already self-medicated, ask further: 'Which antibiotics and doses have you taken?'
stop_conditions: High-risk sexual behavior history has been clearly elicited and symptoms are typical
Necessary epidemiological history has been collected
The patient refuses to provide further information, but symptoms are sufficient to initiate testing

essential: Pharyngeal swab Neisseria gonorrhoeae nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
Pharyngeal swab bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
if_suspected: Syphilis serology
HIV antibody test
Chlamydia nucleic acid amplification test
avoid: Empirical use of broad-spectrum antibiotics before etiological testing
Diagnosis based solely on visual observation of pharyngeal redness and swelling

first_line: First-line: ceftriaxone sodium 1g single intramuscular injection. If concomitant Chlamydia trachomatis infection has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Avoid sexual activity during treatment until symptoms resolve and repeat testing is negative. Non-pharmacological interventions include adequate rest and increased water intake.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated in patients allergic to cephalosporins; assess history of penicillin allergy
Avoid combination with aminoglycosides to prevent increased ototoxicity
Be alert for severe allergic reactions such as anaphylactic shock; observe the patient after administration
personalization: Pregnant women: ceftriaxone is first-line; doxycycline is contraindicated and should be replaced with azithromycin
In renal impairment, adjust the ceftriaxone dose according to creatinine clearance
In children, calculate the ceftriaxone dose by body weight, usually 50-100mg/kg as a single dose

skills.presentation: Patients often present with sudden fever, accompanied by oral mucosal herpes or ulcers leading to refusal to eat and drooling. Maculopapular rash or small vesicles appear on the hands, feet, and buttocks; the rash is not itchy and has an erythematous halo. Some children may have upper respiratory symptoms such as cough and runny nose. If persistent high fever, lethargy, limb trembling, or tachypnea occurs, it suggests possible progression to severe disease.

first_questions: Has your child had fever in the last 3 days? What was the highest temperature?
Have red bumps or blisters appeared on the hands, feet, and buttocks?
Is your child unwilling to eat or drink because of mouth pain?
followup_questions: If fever lasts more than 3 days, ask further: What is the mental status? Is there startle or limb trembling?
If the rash is obvious, ask further: Is the rash itchy? Has it ruptured or become infected?
Ask about recent contact with similar cases at kindergarten or childcare.
stop_conditions: Typical rash distribution (hands, feet, mouth, buttocks) has been confirmed and there are no neurological symptoms.
Epidemiological history investigation and baseline vital sign assessment have been completed.
Parents have mastered key points of home care and confirmed no severe disease warning signs.

essential: Complete blood count
C-reactive protein test
Throat swab enterovirus nucleic acid amplification test
if_suspected: Cerebrospinal fluid examination (when central nervous system involvement is suspected)
Cranial MRI or electroencephalography (when encephalitis is suspected)
Myocardial enzyme panel and electrocardiogram (when myocarditis is suspected)
avoid: Routine use of antibiotics (unless there is evidence of bacterial coinfection)
Unnecessary chest CT (no imaging needed for mild cases)
Repeated invasive procedures (e.g., lumbar puncture only for severe disease indications)

first_line: Mainly symptomatic supportive treatment. For fever above 38.5°C, acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be used to reduce fever

Oral pain can be relieved with lidocaine gel to ease difficulty eating; encourage small, frequent sips of water to prevent dehydration. Keep the skin clean and avoid scratching the rash open. The usual course is 7-10 days and self-resolves; no specific antiviral drugs are needed.
safety_warnings: Aspirin must not be used to reduce fever in children because of the risk of Reye syndrome
Be alert for dehydration risk; avoid forced feeding that may cause choking
Closely observe changes in condition to prevent progression to severe encephalitis or pulmonary edema
personalization: In infants and young children, calculate antipyretic doses precisely by body weight
Children with malnutrition or immunodeficiency should have prolonged isolation and enhanced monitoring
Pregnant contacts should be assessed for fetal risk and consult obstetrics

skills.presentation: Patients often present with subacute or chronic respiratory symptoms, such as persistent dry cough, fever, night sweats, and chest pain, and are easily misdiagnosed as pulmonary tuberculosis. Severe cases may have generalized fatigue and weight loss, with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. If dissemination occurs, skin ulcers, mucosal lesions, or central nervous system symptoms may be seen. The history often includes travel to the Americas (e.g., the Ohio River Valley) or exposure to contaminated soil or bat guano.

first_questions: Have you ever traveled to or lived in the Midwestern United States or Central and South America?
Have you recently been exposed to caves, bat guano, or disturbed soil in old buildings?
How long have the cough and fever lasted, and do you have night sweats?
followup_questions: If you have a rash or oral ulcer, where exactly is it located?
Do you have unexplained significant weight loss or extreme fatigue?
Do you have a history of tuberculosis or immunocompromising conditions (such as HIV, organ transplantation)?
stop_conditions: Epidemiological exposure history has been clearly established and typical respiratory symptoms have lasted more than 2 weeks.
The patient already has clear disseminated symptoms (such as hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions).
Immune status assessment has been completed and initial imaging suggests pulmonary infiltrates.

essential: Chest X-ray or CT
Fungal culture (blood, bone marrow, or sputum)
Urine antigen test (Histoplasma antigen)
if_suspected: Serological antibody testing (complement fixation test, immunodiffusion)
Bone marrow aspiration smear and culture
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) microscopy and culture
avoid: Long-term empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics without indications
Unnecessary invasive biopsy (when antigen testing is positive)
Relying solely on tuberculin skin test for differential diagnosis

first_line: Mild to moderate cases: oral itraconazole is first-line, 200mg three times daily for 6-12 months

Severe or disseminated cases: liposomal amphotericin B intravenous infusion is first-line (0.7-1.0 mg/kg/d), followed by sequential oral itraconazole consolidation therapy after the condition stabilizes. At the same time, nutritional support should be strengthened and fatigue avoided. The course of treatment should be dynamically adjusted according to clinical symptom improvement and the decline in antigen titers.
safety_warnings: Amphotericin B is nephrotoxic; renal function and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) need to be monitored.
Itraconazole carries a risk of cardiotoxicity; use with caution in patients with heart failure, and it has interactions with many drugs.
A Jarisch-Herxheimer-like reaction may occur early in treatment; vital signs should be closely observed.
personalization: HIV-infected patients require combined antiretroviral therapy and a prolonged antifungal course.
Itraconazole is contraindicated in pregnant women; amphotericin B is first-line, but fetal risk must be weighed.
In hepatic impairment, adjust the itraconazole dose and closely monitor liver enzymes.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of long-term fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, and pallor, suggesting iron-deficiency anemia. Some patients have a history of skin itching or rash (such as 'ground itch'), mostly occurring after barefoot contact with soil. Gastrointestinal symptoms include vague epigastric pain, abnormal appetite, or pica (craving soil or raw rice). Severe cases may develop lower limb edema and manifestations of heart failure. Symptoms are insidious and easily mistaken for ordinary anemia or malnutrition.

first_questions: Have you ever walked barefoot in farmland or moist soil?
Recently, have you felt unusually tired, palpitations, or pale?
Do you have a habit of eating soil, ice, or raw rice?
followup_questions: If skin itching or a red rash occurs, please describe the site and duration.
Has your stool color turned black or tarry? Do you have abdominal pain or diarrhea?
Have you had significant recent weight loss or lower limb swelling?
stop_conditions: Barefoot exposure history has been clearly established and typical anemia and gastrointestinal symptoms are present
Stool examination has confirmed hookworm eggs positive
The patient has no new symptoms and the previous confirmed diagnosis and treatment history is clear

essential: Routine stool examination (direct smear method)
Complete blood count (focus on hemoglobin and hematocrit)
Serum ferritin test
if_suspected: Duodenal aspirate examination (for parasite localization)
Electrocardiogram (to assess myocardial ischemia due to anemia)
Occult blood test (to exclude other gastrointestinal bleeding)
avoid: Blind performance of gastrointestinal endoscopy (when there is no indication)
Nonspecific antibiotic treatment
Repeated imaging examinations without clinical significance

first_line: First-line: albendazole 400mg orally once daily for 3 days

Or mebendazole 100mg orally twice daily for 3 days. At the same time, iron supplements (such as ferrous sulfate 0.3g three times daily) and vitamin C should be added to promote absorption; the course depends on the severity of anemia and usually needs to continue until hemoglobin returns to normal. Improving sanitation and avoiding barefoot contact with soil are recommended.
safety_warnings: Use albendazole with caution in pregnant and breastfeeding women; contraindicated in early pregnancy
In hepatic impairment, monitor liver enzymes and avoid concomitant use of hepatotoxic drugs
Be alert for allergic reactions; observe for 30 minutes after the first dose to prevent anaphylactic shock
personalization: In children, adjust the dose by body weight (15mg/kg/day), given in divided doses
In severe anemia, correct hypoxia before deworming to prevent worsening of the condition
In older patients, pay attention to comorbidity management and avoid drug interactions

skills.presentation: Patients often present with asymptomatic dull pain in the hepatic region or abdomen and abdominal distension; some have a palpable painless, hard, smooth-surfaced mass. If the cyst ruptures, sudden severe abdominal pain, anaphylactic shock, or secondary infection causing fever may occur. Patients with pulmonary disease may have cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. The history often includes living in pastoral areas or contact with dogs and sheep.

first_questions: Have you ever lived long-term in a pastoral area or had close contact with dogs or sheep?
Recently, have you felt persistent dull pain or fullness in the right upper abdomen or chest?
Have previous physical examinations ever found a cystic space-occupying lesion in the liver or lungs?
followup_questions: If you have sudden severe pain or difficulty breathing, does the pain radiate? Have you coughed up white cyst fluid?
If you can feel a mass, how quickly is its size changing? Is it accompanied by fever or jaundice?
If pulmonary involvement is suspected, is your cough accompanied by blood-streaked sputum or copious frothy sputum?
stop_conditions: Clear epidemiological history (pastoral area/dog or sheep contact) has been established and imaging shows typical cystic lesions
Serologic testing (e.g., ELISA) has been completed and the result is strongly positive
The patient has emergency manifestations of cyst rupture and requires immediate surgical referral

essential: Abdominal or chest ultrasonography (preferred screening)
Serum hydatid antibody testing (ELISA or IHA)
CT or MRI (to assess cyst location, size, and complications)
if_suspected: Chest X-ray (to evaluate for pulmonary echinococcosis)
Complete liver function tests (to assess biliary obstruction or liver injury)
Needle biopsy (only when rupture risk has been rigorously assessed as absent and the diagnosis is unclear)
avoid: Routine percutaneous aspiration (strictly prohibited before drug pretreatment to prevent anaphylactic shock)
Unnecessary invasive biopsy (high risk of hypersensitivity)
Blind use of antibiotic therapy (ineffective against parasites)

first_line: Oral albendazole is the first-line treatment; adults usually receive 400 mg twice daily for 3-6 months, with perioperative combination therapy to kill daughter cysts. For a single, localized, uncomplicated cyst, the PAIR technique (puncture, aspiration, injection of a protoscolicidal agent, and reaspiration) may be performed. Surgical resection is indicated for giant cysts, multivesicular cysts, or those complicated by biliary obstruction. Liver function and complete blood count should be monitored simultaneously.
safety_warnings: Puncture is strictly prohibited without prophylactic antiparasitic therapy to prevent cyst fluid spillage causing anaphylactic shock
Albendazole is hepatotoxic; liver function must be monitored regularly during treatment, and concomitant use with metabolism-affecting drugs such as cimetidine should be avoided
Albendazole is contraindicated in pregnant women and children under 2 years of age, and should be used with caution in breastfeeding women
personalization: Pediatric patients require precise weight-based dosing and close monitoring of growth and development parameters
Patients with hepatic impairment require dose reduction or temporary discontinuation, with regimen adjustment after recovery
Immunosuppressed patients require a prolonged course and combined immunomodulatory therapy

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden high fever, marked sore throat with difficulty swallowing, and cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy (especially prominent in the posterior cervical triangle); some have fatigue, rash, and hepatosplenomegaly. Symptoms resemble a cold, but pharyngeal congestion is more severe, and tonsillar exudate may be seen. The course usually lasts 2-4 weeks and is more common in adolescents; vigilance for risk of airway obstruction is required.

first_questions: Have you had a persistent fever for more than 3 days accompanied by severe sore throat?
Recently, have you had cervical lymph node enlargement or extreme fatigue?
followup_questions: If a rash has appeared, did it occur after you took antibiotics?
Do you have left upper abdominal pain, which may suggest an enlarged spleen?
stop_conditions: Typical triad (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy) has been clearly established
Complete blood count and EBV antibody results are available and confirm the diagnosis
Other serious complications such as airway obstruction have been excluded

essential: Peripheral blood smear (proportion of atypical lymphocytes)
Epstein-Barr virus serology (VCA-IgM/IgG)
Liver function tests
if_suspected: Abdominal ultrasonography (to assess spleen size)
Chest X-ray (to evaluate for mediastinal lymphadenopathy)
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (not a bacterial infection)
Unnecessary CT scanning (radiation exposure and unnecessary)
